scenes.tts: A whale looks more like a tuna than a hippo. So why does the family tree pair whale with hippo? Shape offers one clue, but ancestry can leave a different pattern. Watch which features travel together through the branches.
scenes.caption: A whale looks more like a tuna than a hippo. So why does the family tree pair whale with hippo? Shape offers one clue, but ancestry can leave a different pattern. Watch which features travel together through the branches.
scenes.visual: COLOR MAP for both films: whale BLUE, hippo GREEN, tuna GREY, inherited evidence TEAL, common ancestors and branch points GOLD. Begin underwater with a large blue whale and grey tuna swimming in parallel; a green hippo walks through a river panel. Their silhouettes enlarge to fill most of the frame. A dotted bracket links whale and tuna by shape, while a gold question mark pulses between whale and hippo. Water and bubbles drift throughout. Mark all animal drawings 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: A whale looks more like a tuna than a hippo. So why does the family tree pair whale with hippo? Shape offers one clue, but ancestry can leave a different pattern. Watch which features travel together through the branches.

scenes.visual: Keep the three moving animals dimly visible. Bring in the title 'Which Similarities Reveal Relatives?' for two seconds, then transform its underline into the first branch of a tree.

scenes.tts: Whales and tuna both move through water. A smooth body and fins help both animals swim. Similar conditions can favour similar solutions, even in groups that are not close relatives. Scientists therefore ask a sharper question. Which similarities were inherited from a shared ancestor?
scenes.caption: Whales and tuna both move through water. A smooth body and fins help both animals swim. Similar conditions can favour similar solutions, even in groups that are not close relatives. Scientists therefore ask a sharper question. Which similarities were inherited from a shared ancestor?
scenes.visual: Carry the whale and tuna forward. Flow lines stream around both bodies as they swim; label the shared outline 'swimming shape'. Then peel that outline away into a grey card labelled 'same job'. A teal magnifying beam scans inside each animal, replacing the grey shape bracket with the question 'inherited together?' The hippo remains moving slowly in its river at frame right.
scenes.narration: Whales and tuna both move through water. A smooth body and fins help both animals swim. Similar conditions can favour similar solutions, even in groups that are not close relatives. Scientists therefore ask a sharper question. Which similarities were inherited from a shared ancestor?

scenes.tts: Suppose you could follow only one trail. Would you choose the outside shape, or features passed through generations? Hold your answer. The useful trail should explain several different observations, not just one resemblance.
scenes.caption: Suppose you could follow only one trail. Would you choose the outside shape, or features passed through generations? Hold your answer. The useful trail should explain several different observations, not just one resemblance.
scenes.visual: Split one wide trail into a GREY route labelled 'outside shape' and a TEAL route labelled 'inherited features'. Place the whale icon at the fork. Keep both routes gently flowing toward two covered tree silhouettes. End with the question large and centred; do not reveal a route yet.
scenes.narration: Suppose you could follow only one trail. Would you choose the outside shape, or features passed through generations? Hold your answer. The useful trail should explain several different observations, not just one resemblance.

scenes.visual: Keep the question and both routes visible. The whale bobs gently while small dots move down each route. No answer highlight appears during the thinking pause.

scenes.tts: Start inside the front limb. A human hand, bat wing, and whale flipper do different jobs. Yet each keeps the same basic bone pattern. Matching parts shift into new shapes without losing their order. That pattern is a homologous structure, inherited from a common ancestor.
scenes.caption: Start inside the front limb. A human hand, bat wing, and whale flipper do different jobs. Yet each keeps the same basic bone pattern. Matching parts shift into new shapes without losing their order. That pattern is a homologous structure, inherited from a common ancestor.
scenes.visual: The teal route opens. Build one large schematic forelimb from labelled blocks: 'upper arm', 'forearm pair', 'wrist', 'fingers'. Duplicate it three times in the same positions. Smoothly reshape the outlines into a hand, bat wing and whale flipper while the four labelled blocks remain aligned and teal. Gold paths converge backward to one ancestor circle.
scenes.narration: Start inside the front limb. A human hand, bat wing, and whale flipper do different jobs. Yet each keeps the same basic bone pattern. Matching parts shift into new shapes without losing their order. That pattern is a homologous structure, inherited from a common ancestor.

scenes.tts: Development and fossils add other views. Vertebrate embryos can begin with shared parts, then follow different paths. Fossils place past body forms in time order. Whale embryos begin hind limbs, and fossil whales had working legs. Neither clue depends on an adult whale looking like a fish.
scenes.caption: Development and fossils add other views. Vertebrate embryos can begin with shared parts, then follow different paths. Fossils place past body forms in time order. Whale embryos begin hind limbs, and fossil whales had working legs. Neither clue depends on an adult whale looking like a fish.
scenes.visual: Transform the forelimb blocks into three large schematic embryo silhouettes sharing teal tail and arch marks; then let their later outlines diverge. Slide in a horizontal rock-layer timeline labelled 'past' to 'present'. Show a schematic four-legged fossil whale on the older layer and a modern whale on the present layer, joined by branching lines to a shared GOLD node. Do not morph one into the other. Keep the word 'schematic' on both embryo and fossil panels.
scenes.narration: Development and fossils add other views. Vertebrate embryos can begin with shared parts, then follow different paths. Fossils place past body forms in time order. Whale embryos begin hind limbs, and fossil whales had working legs. Neither clue depends on an adult whale looking like a fish.

scenes.tts: D N A supplies another record. Scientists compare corresponding sequences and look for changes inherited together. Shared insertions at matching locations are especially useful clues. Several such clues place whales beside hippos. When body, embryo, fossil, and D N A evidence agree, the grouping becomes stronger.
scenes.caption: DNA supplies another record. Scientists compare corresponding sequences and look for changes inherited together. Shared insertions at matching locations are especially useful clues. Several such clues place whales beside hippos. When body, embryo, fossil, and DNA evidence agree, the grouping becomes stronger.
scenes.visual: Keep the timeline and transform it into five straight aligned sequence strips labelled whale, hippo, pig, cow and 'outgroup'. Do not draw molecular structure. Teal rectangular insertion blocks slide into the same matching positions at several spots on the whale and hippo strips only; the pig, cow and outgroup strips stay empty at those spots. The strips fold into branches, with whale and hippo meeting at a shared gold node and pig and cow branching earlier. Four evidence icons orbit that node and lock into one teal ring.
scenes.narration: DNA supplies another record. Scientists compare corresponding sequences and look for changes inherited together. Shared insertions at matching locations are especially useful clues. Several such clues place whales beside hippos. When body, embryo, fossil, and DNA evidence agree, the grouping becomes stronger.

scenes.tts: One clue can be incomplete, so scientists compare independent evidence. Body structures, development, fossils, and D N A test the same branches from different angles. When they agree, the grouping gains support. The useful traits are derived traits. A derived trait first appeared in one ancestor and passed to its descendants. Trace shared derived traits to branch points to find the closest relatives.

scenes.visual: Pull back from the whale-hippo node until the full schematic tree fills the frame. Four TEAL evidence paths, labelled 'body', 'development', 'fossils' and 'DNA', approach the same GOLD node from different directions. They lock into one ring around the node. A TEAL tile labelled 'derived trait: first in one ancestor' settles on the branch just before the whale-hippo node. Then a tracer follows that mark to the branch point while the full rule appears once.

When they agree, the grouping gains support. The useful traits are derived traits. A derived trait first appeared in one ancestor and passed to its descendants. Trace shared derived traits to branch points to find the closest relatives.

scenes.tts: Now the first question has an answer. The whale's swimming shape links it to tuna by function. Its lungs, limb bones, and embryos link it to four-limbed land animals. Its milk, fossils, and D N A link it to mammals. Within living mammals, the evidence places whales closest to hippos. The tree records ancestry, not overall appearance.

scenes.visual: Return to the opening world. Fade the grey whale-tuna shape bracket but keep it labelled 'function'. Grow a large tree from the gold node: tuna on an earlier branch, whale and hippo on branches sharing a later gold node. Teal evidence symbols travel down the whale path and settle before that shared node. Do not label any group 'only', 'rejected' or 'more advanced'.

scenes.tts: Looks still matter when they preserve inherited parts. They mislead when a shared job produces a similar form. So begin with traits, test them with independent evidence, and follow their paths toward shared ancestors. That turns a resemblance into a claim you can check.

scenes.visual: On the same tree, the grey shape card becomes a small side note while the teal evidence path brightens. A finger-like tracer starts at whale, moves toward the root and pauses at the gold whale-hippo node. The camera eases out so the full branching picture fills the frame. Ambient water motion continues behind the tree.

scenes.visual: Clear everything to one centred line only: 'Trace shared derived traits to branch points to find the closest relatives.' Keep the line in TEAL with one thin GOLD branching stroke behind it. No subtitle, logo, smaller line or extra takeaway.
